Geek
GEEK
noun (Gen X slang)
From English and Scots geck, a fool or dupe (from Low German / Dutch geck; Shakespeare’s Malvolio complains of being made "the most notorious geck and gull" in Twelfth Night). In the early 20th-century American carnival a geek was the lowest sideshow performer, billed as a "wild man" who did degrading stunts for a crowd, a figure made famous by the novel and film Nightmare Alley (1946, 1947). By mid-century it was a schoolboy insult for an odd or awkward person; in the late 1970s and 1980s, with the personal computer, it took on its Gen X sense — a brilliant, socially awkward enthusiast, the computer geek — and Anthony Michael Hall’s character in Sixteen Candles (1984) is credited simply as "The Geek." The 1990s tech boom turned it into a badge of honor.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A geek began as the lowest act in the carnival and ended as the man who builds the software. In between, Gen X used it for the boy with the pocket protector and the home computer, the one who could program in BASIC but could not talk to girls. By the 1990s the geeks were building the future and the word had become a badge: "I’m a total history geek." The Christian observation is that God made the kind of mind that geeks out, and He gave it something worth searching. "The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein" (Psa 111:2). "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter" (Pro 25:2). When God built His tabernacle, He filled Bezaleel "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3), and He gave Daniel and his friends "knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom" (Dan 1:17). Deep focus, love of detail, delight in how things work — these are gifts. The old meaning of the word still has a lesson, too: a geck was a fool, and the apostle gladly wore the name: "We are fools for Christ’s sake" (1Co 4:10). A father can tell his geeky son: your mind is made in the image of a God who delights in detail; use it to study His works, serve His people, and do not be ashamed to look foolish for Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

From geck (a fool) through the carnival sideshow to the Gen X computer geek (1980s) — the awkward enthusiast turned badge of honor; Scripture: the works of the LORD are sought out of all them that have pleasure therein (Psa 111:2).

GEEK, n. (Gen X slang, 1980s sense, United States) A socially awkward person with intense, often technical, enthusiasms; a computer expert. "Ask the geek in third period to fix it."

Compounds and forms: computer geek, history geek, geek out (to enthuse at length), geeky; reclaimed as a badge of honor in the 1990s tech boom.

Earlier senses: a carnival sideshow "wild man" (early 20th c.); a fool or dupe (geck, 16th c.).

Webster 1828: GECK, n. A dupe.

Decode for parents: a geeky child has a God-given appetite for detail; aim it at the works of the LORD (Psa 111:2).

Key Scripture

Psa 111:2 — "The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein."

Pro 25:2 — "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter."

Exo 31:3 — "And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,"

Dan 1:17 — "As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams."

1Co 4:10 — "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised."

Modern Corruption

Geek once mocked the odd and the awkward; reclaimed, it names a love of learning that Scripture honors when it is aimed at the works of God.

expand to see more

From sideshow to badge. The word’s history is a parable. It began with the fool and the carnival "wild man" — a man degraded for a crowd’s amusement — and Gen X hallways used it to push the studious boy to the margins. Then the world discovered it needed him. That reversal is not new: God "hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27), and Paul was content to be counted a fool for Christ’s sake (1Co 4:10).

The temptation of the redeemed word. Now that geek is a badge, it has its own danger: knowledge that puffs up, and a life poured into screens, games, and trivia while the weightier matters wait. Bezaleel’s skill was for the tabernacle (Exo 31:3); Daniel’s learning served a God he prayed to three times a day (Dan 1:17). The best geek is the one who searches out the works of the LORD with pleasure (Psa 111:2) and gives Him the glory.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Low German / Dutch geck (fool) → English geck (Shakespeare) → carnival geek (early 1900s) → schoolboy insult → 1980s computer geek → 1990s badge of honor; Scripture: search out a matter (Pro 25:2).
